Beverages / Campaign & packaging

Share a Coke gives the buyer someone to look for

Putting a name on the bottle changes the shopping question, then gives the answer somewhere to travel.

2026-09-16Independent analysis

BRAND
COCA-COLA

ANALYSIS
CAMPAIGN & PACKAGING

A Coke is usually bought for a moment. A Coke with somebody's name on it is bought for a person. That tiny change has always been the best part of Share a Coke for me, and it is why the 2025 return deserves more attention than a nostalgia headline.

The pack becomes the invitation

Coca-Cola brought first names back to cans and bottles in 2025. The company said the rollout would reach more than 120 countries; its second-quarter release reported over 30,000 locally tailored names across roughly 10 billion packs. Those figures describe extraordinary scale. The mechanic, though, works at the scale of one friend spotting another friend's name.

A shelf turns into a search

I think that changes the shelf from a display of identical SKUs into a small search. You look for your own name, then perhaps someone else's. A routine purchase gets a recipient, and the packaging supplies the story you might tell when you hand it over.

  • A name makes the product easier to photograph and send.
  • The physical pack gives the recipient something tangible.
  • The search itself gives a shopper one more reason to scan the shelf.

What happens when your name is missing?

This is the fault line in personalization at scale. A shopper who cannot find the right name may feel the campaign is for other people. Coca-Cola's 2025 digital hub, reached through its app and on-pack QR codes, offered more names and shareable video creation. I read that as a way to extend participation beyond the names a store can stock.

A question I would ask

Does the digital option rescue the disappointment of an absent name, or does it feel like homework after the shelf has already let you down?

The company's materials prove distribution and describe the experience; they do not prove that names caused incremental sales. I would compare gifting intent and actual purchase across named packs, customizable digital packs and standard packs, especially for people who did not find the name they wanted. That is where the promise of inclusion meets the reality of a SKU.

SOURCE NOTES

What the sources can and cannot tell us

Coca-Cola reports the campaign's mechanics and scale. The claim that names change search and gifting behaviour is my interpretation; these public sources do not isolate incremental sales from personalization.
